title: How to read a cross-stitch chart
subtitle: The grid, the symbols, and the colour key
excerpt: A cross-stitch chart is a square grid where each filled square represents one stitch. Symbols or shaded blocks indicate thread colours; the colour key at the edge of the chart gives the thread code for each symbol. Reading the chart means counting squares, not following a picture.
sourceNotes: Chart-reading conventions are universal across counted cross-stitch traditions. The grid-and-key format is documented in The Priscilla needlework books (1900s), available via the Internet Archive. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, covers the charted method in the cross-stitch chapter.
aliases: how to use cross stitch chart

glossaryTerms.definition: Cross-stitch worked from a gridded chart by counting squares rather than following a printed design on the fabric. The stitcher counts the Aida squares against the chart squares to place each stitch correctly. This method gives precise, repeatable results on any fabric count.

content.text: A cross-stitch chart is a grid where each square corresponds to one Aida square on your fabric. A symbol, colour block, or shade inside the chart square tells you what stitch to make and in which thread.
means you count the grid rather than following a stamped design on the fabric. The count is exact: one chart square equals one Aida square.

The colour key lives at the edge of the chart. It lists every symbol or shade that appears in the grid alongside the thread brand and code number. Most published charts give both the DMC and Anchor codes for each colour. Before starting, check which brand you have and read from the correct column.
The main body of the chart. Each square is one full cross-stitch. Thicker lines divide the grid into blocks of ten squares to make counting easier.

The chart marks each colour with a unique symbol or shade. Common symbols are crosses, dots, diagonal lines, and letters. Some charts use coloured squares directly, which is easier to read but harder to print.

Most charts mark the exact centre of the design with arrows or a cross on the margin. Find this point first and mark the corresponding centre of your fabric with a fold or a removable pen. All counting starts from the centre outward.

Always start from the centre of the chart, not the top-left corner. Fold the fabric in quarters to find its centre, then mark it. Find the matching centre mark on the chart. Work outward from the centre in all directions. This ensures the design lands in the middle of your fabric with equal margins on all sides.

Use a transparent ruler, a highlighter strip, or a magnetic chart holder to track your row on the chart. Mark each completed row with a removable highlighter pen on the printed chart. Check the fabric against the chart every ten to fifteen stitches: catching a counting error early costs far less than unpicking a whole section.
